text.p: This is how major world bond markets were trading in late European business on Friday.

GERMANY - Bund futures were lower in late trade after swinging in a wild 70-point range on the back of U.S. data which also shook the Treasury market. The DTB December Bund future was down 33 basis points in 1335 GMT at 99.30, down sharply from an earlier upward spike that saw the contract hit a contract high of 100.01. The September Bund future on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) was trading at 99.51, down 0.09 from Thursday's settlement price.

BRITAIN - Gilts slumped into Friday's close, totally losing momentum and parting company with Bunds which fought back after severe afternoon losses. European markets ratcheted lower on talk of a big seller of five-year German paper and 10-year U.S. T-notes, but the German market fought back after a savage 75 basis point fall from the day's high. The September long gilt future on LIFFE was trading at 108-22/32, down 20/32 from Thursday's settlement price.

UNITED STATES - U.S. Treasuries edged lower in busy midday trade as several factors dragged prices down from an early rally on October employment data, analysts said. The September Treasury bond future on the Chicago Board of Trade was trading at 113-2/32, up 2/32 from Thursday's settlement price. The long bond was quoted to yield 6.65 percent.

JAPAN - Key December Japanese government bond futures ended slightly lower on Friday after setting an all-time high earlier in the afternoon. The December contract fell rapidly toward the close due to position adjustment sales ahead of a long weekend, a brokerage. In after hours trading the June future on LIFFE was trading at 125.26, down 0.16 from Thursday's settlement price on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

EUROBONDS - LONDON - The Eurobond market was subdued on Friday after a hectic week due to holidays in much of Europe and in anticipation of October U.S. jobs data due for release later. Dealers said the figures would be closely watched. A Reuter poll of economists showed an average forecast of a 212,000 gain in October non-farm payrolls, compared with September's 40,000 fall.
